solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Message from above heralded by 100 saucer-shaped craft?

indicators.note: a herald goes ahead announcing what follows, so the 100 comes before the message

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
an oracle is a pronouncement from the gods

explanation.surface: A UFO sighting: a flying saucer arrives bearing word from the heavens.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: 'saucer-shaped craft' looks like a flying saucer but is a coracle, a round wicker boat paddled on Welsh rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: A description by shape: the coracle is a small round boat, bowl-like as a saucer.

clue.text: Detour in force — it's marked by cones

indicators.note: a detour takes a different route, so the letters of IN FORCE go a different way round

explanation.surface: Roadworks: a diversion is in operation and the route is lined with traffic cones.
explanation.walkthrough: The cones look like the plastic ones of a road diversion; they are pine cones.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by distinguishing feature: bearing cones is what makes a tree a conifer.

clue.text: One releasing locks to allow access to tower?

definitions.text: One releasing locks to allow access to tower?

parts.note: the surface pictures a keyholder undoing door locks; the setter means someone letting down locks of hair
the hair is let down as a ladder so a visitor can climb up into the tower

explanation.surface: A jailer unlocking the doors of a tower.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Grimm fairy tale Rapunzel is shut in a doorless tower and lets down her long hair for the prince to climb.
explanation.definitionFit: A whimsical description of the fairy-tale heroine's defining act.

clue.text: Unit that is led by mounted police no longer active

indicators.note: whatever is led walks behind its leader
something mounted is raised up, and in a down clue that means the letters read upwards

parts.note: the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Northern Ireland's police force until 2001

explanation.surface: A mounted police unit that has been disbanded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mounted police' suggests horses; mounted is the reversal, applied to the RUC, a force that no longer exists.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific example of a unit: the curie is an old measure of radioactivity named after Marie and Pierre Curie.

clue.text: Broadcast of next episode having turned out so timely

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it, so the letters are scattered
to turn someone out is to evict them, so SO is thrown out of the fodder

parts.note: S and O are removed, leaving NEXTEPIDE to rearrange

explanation.surface: A trailer for the next episode of a series goes out at just the right moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So timely' seems a single phrase; SO belongs to the wordplay and only 'timely' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: what is expedient suits the moment, as a timely act does.

clue.text: Bowman's instrument for withdrawing arrows

indicators.note: to withdraw is to draw back, so the word is drawn back and runs the other way

parts.note: a Strad (Stradivarius) is a violin, played by a man with a bow

explanation.surface: An archer's bow, used for pulling arrows back to shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: The bowman seems to be an archer; he is a violinist.
explanation.definitionFit: Pub slang: darts players call their darts arrows.

clue.text: Party drugs a turn-up for the books? The opposite

definitions.text: a turn-up for the books? The opposite

explanation.surface: A party where drugs turn up is a surprising turn of events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A turn-up for the books' is British slang for a surprise, which the drugs at the party seem to be; read literally and reversed, it becomes a turn-down in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading of an idiom, inverted: a dog-ear is a page corner turned down in a book.

clue.text: Take over again on parking in a small spot

parts.note: a dot is a small spot
P = parking, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Someone looking for a tiny parking space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parking in a small spot' reads as a driver squeezing into a space, which is exactly the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to readopt is to adopt, take over, once more.

clue.text: Revolutionary is fool to back strike action

indicators.note: a revolution is a turn, so IS is turned round

explanation.surface: A radical denounced as an idiot for supporting industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a noun for an activist; it is an instruction to turn IS round.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind of strike: in a sit-in workers occupy the premises instead of working.

clue.text: My order turned up around noon from North Africa

indicators.note: turned upside down in a down clue, the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: cor! is a British exclamation like 'my!'
the OM is the Order of Merit
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A diner's meal finally arrives at around twelve, from a North African kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My order' reads as a meal; 'My' is the exclamation and 'order' the honour, together turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective by origin: Morocco lies in North Africa.

clue.text: Admit wrongdoing by publisher binding opponents in contract

indicators.note: a binding wraps round what it holds

parts.note: in contract bridge, West and North are opponents

explanation.surface: A publishing house confesses to trapping its rivals in a legal agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks legal; it is contract bridge, whose players sit at the compass points, so any two neighbours are opponents.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: to own up is to confess a fault.

clue.text: Disgusting ruling backed up boards

indicators.note: backed means moved in reverse, so UP runs backwards
to board a ship is to get inside it

explanation.surface: An offensive decision is upheld by the directors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boards' looks like company directors; it is a verb, the reversed UP climbing aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: repugnant things arouse disgust.

clue.text: Wrong of church to take possession of flat

explanation.surface: A church seizing someone's apartment is a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' reads as an apartment; it is flat wetland, as in the Fens of eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun synonym: an offence is a wrong done, a breach of law or morals.

clue.text: Battle-axe catching old cavalryman

parts.note: a battle-axe or dragon is a fierce woman

explanation.surface: A fierce old woman seizes an elderly soldier on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battle-axe' looks like a weapon a cavalryman might carry; it is a formidable woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific kind of cavalryman: dragoons were soldiers who rode to battle.

clue.text: Assortment of bread enclosed in oriental dishes

parts.note: enc. = enclosed, as at the foot of a letter

explanation.surface: A selection of breads served alongside curries.
explanation.walkthrough: The breads look like naan and chapati to go with the curries; 'bread' is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: bread is money, and an assortment of monies is several currencies.

clue.text: Lift installed by minder who's taken over running the estate?

definitions.text: who's taken over running the estate?
definitions.note: the definition is a relative clause; read it as 'one who's taken over'

indicators.note: something installed is fitted inside, so the lift goes inside the minder

explanation.surface: A new caretaker has been put in to run a country estate.
explanation.walkthrough: The estate is an estate car (a station wagon), and taking over running it means stealing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description by example: a carjacker seizes a car, such as an estate, and drives it.

clue.text: Winger's going over for try

indicators.note: something going over flips, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a bat is a winger, a winged creature; BAT'S = bat is

explanation.surface: A rugby winger crosses the line to score a try.
explanation.walkthrough: The rugby surface makes 'try' a score; it means an attempt, and the winger is a bat.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: having a stab at something means attempting it.

clue.text: Attractive person keeping company with maiden

explanation.surface: A charming person who spends time with a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeping company with' reads as courting; the phrase splits into the container instruction and the letters it holds.
explanation.definitionFit: An older sense: a becoming dress is one that flatters, making its wearer attractive.

clue.text: India allowed to detain politician without need for express statement

indicators.note: to detain someone is to hold them

parts.note: I is India in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: India is permitted to hold a politician without charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests detention without trial; the definition is the whole last phrase, meaning understood but unsaid.
explanation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: what is implicit is understood without being spelled out.

clue.text: One of A to G? Yes and no

definitions.text: One of A to G? Yes and no

parts.note: the surface reads as a letter of the alphabet; in music the letters A to G name the steps of the scale
the answer both is one of A to G and, split in two, denies being a certain letter among them

explanation.surface: A quiz question answered with a shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: The notes of the scale are named A to G, so 'yes'; but NOTE also splits as NOT E, refusing one of those letters, so 'no'.
explanation.definitionFit: A description by naming convention: musical notes are labelled with the letters A to G.

clue.text: Senator charged for attempting to overthrow government?

indicators.note: charged particles are agitated, so the letters of SENATOR are stirred up

explanation.surface: A senator is indicted for plotting a coup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' belongs so naturally to the courtroom story that it hides its job as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: treason is the crime of betraying or trying to topple one's own state.

clue.text: Irish, making a comeback in tight match, tie 1-1?

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way it came, so IR runs backwards

parts.note: MATCH TIE rearranged, with RI going in after the A

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another
tight is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of order

explanation.surface: An Irish team fights back in a close game to draw one-all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight match' looks like a close game, and '1-1' like the score; 1-1 is a sum.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one minus one is a small sum, a piece of arithmetic.

clue.text: Extremists in theory oversaw New York's oppressive system

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its ends, so take the first and last letters of 'theory'

explanation.surface: Theoretical radicals supervised a harsh New York regime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' reads as radicals; it means the extreme letters of the next word. The 's is 'is', linking wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: tyranny is a system of cruel, absolute rule.

clue.text: Parisian who cut a piece of cake is feeling sick

indicators.note: a cut word is trimmed short, so QUI loses its last letter

parts.note: qui is French for who; cut, it loses the I
a piece of cake is something easy

explanation.surface: A Frenchman who took a slice of gâteau now feels ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut a piece of cake' reads as one action; 'cut' works on the French word, and 'a piece of cake' is an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: queasy describes the nausea of feeling sick.

clue.text: Mirrors used for inspecting upscale complex

indicators.note: complex means intricate, tangled, so the letters of UPSCALE are tangled

explanation.surface: Mirrors fitted for viewings at an upmarket housing development.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complex' looks like a building development; it is the anagram signal. Specula is the Latin plural of speculum.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical term: a speculum is a mirror or medical instrument for examining body cavities.

clue.text: Part of wicket test umpire checks

indicators.note: to check is to hold back, so the phrase holds the answer inside it

explanation.surface: A Test match umpire inspecting the wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a Test is an international match and the wicket is three upright posts topped by bails, so the surface never leaves the field.
explanation.definitionFit: A part for the whole: a stump is one of the three posts that make a cricket wicket.

clue.text: Irrational learner driver threatening person on the road to Canterbury?

definitions.text: person on the road to Canterbury?

parts.note: British learner drivers display L plates

explanation.surface: A reckless novice at the wheel endangers others on the Canterbury road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irrational' seems to describe the driver; it is a number.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary allusion: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales follows pilgrims travelling to Becket's shrine at Canterbury.

clue.text: Animal expert spending time chasing water bug

indicators.note: what you spend is used up and gone, so VET loses its T

explanation.surface: A zoologist hunts an aquatic insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water bug' reads as an insect; the two words split, water giving letters and bug being the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to bug someone is to irritate them.

clue.text: Loose articles of French clothing shed

indicators.note: clothing wraps round a body

parts.note: un and le are French articles

explanation.surface: Baggy French garments being cast off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose' looks like an adjective for the clothes; it is the verb, as in to loose a prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: An old verb sense: to loose is to release from bonds.

clue.text: Clergyman's piece making a considerable impression in sermon

indicators.note: a sermon is preached out loud, so the word is heard rather than seen

parts.note: a cannon is an artillery piece, whose shot makes a big impression

explanation.surface: A cleric's sermon passage has a strong effect on the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' looks like a passage of the sermon; it is a gun. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific clergyman: a canon is a priest on the staff of a cathedral.

clue.text: Little finger stained by pen on page

indicators.note: in an across clue, A on B means A placed after B, so the stained part follows the page

explanation.surface: A writer's small finger smudged by a pen resting on the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures the ink smudge on a writer's hand; the parts come in reverse order, with the page first.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal, chiefly American and Scottish name for the smallest finger.

clue.text: Frost's never receding with temperature by turn of year coming back down

indicators.note: receding means moving back
a turn spins something round

parts.note: ne'er, the poetic never a poet such as Robert Frost might use

explanation.surface: Frost never lets up as the temperature falls with the year's turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frost' seems like weather; it is the American poet Robert Frost, whose 'never' is the poetic contraction.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical sense: re-entry is a spacecraft's return down into the atmosphere.
